title: Accents de la francophonie
subtitle: Québec, Belgium, Switzerland, the South, Africa

lessons.title: Québec French
lessons.goal: Recognise Québec pronunciation and everyday words.

tip.title: tsu, dzire and long vowels
tip.body: In Québec, t and d before i and u (and before the glides in tiens, dieu) are pronounced with a hiss: tu ≈ "tsu", petit ≈ "p'tsi", dire ≈ "dzire", du ≈ "dzu". Long vowels in a closed syllable are often diphthongised (père, fête, tard), while i, u, ou before a final consonant are often shorter and more relaxed (vite, jupe, route). Informal speech adds a question particle -tu: Tu viens-tu ? Everyday vocabulary differs too: fin de semaine, magasiner, courriel, char, dépanneur — and déjeuner/dîner/souper for breakfast/lunch/dinner.

phrases.t: On se voit en fin de semaine ?
phrases.n: Shall we meet at the weekend?
Are you coming for lunch with us?
phrases.note: Informal Québec: "-tu" marks a yes/no question; dîner = lunch.

lines.name: Sylvie
lines.t: Salut ! Qu'est-ce que tu fais en fin de semaine ?
lines.n: Hi! What are you doing at the weekend?

lines.t: Je vais magasiner au centre-ville. Et toi ?
lines.n: I'm going shopping downtown. And you?

lines.name: Sylvie
lines.t: Rien de spécial. Tu veux-tu dîner avec moi samedi ?
lines.n: Nothing special. Do you want to have lunch with me on Saturday?

lines.t: Avec plaisir ! On se retrouve où ?
lines.n: With pleasure! Where shall we meet?

lines.name: Sylvie
lines.t: Devant le dépanneur, à midi. Je vais venir avec mon char.
lines.n: In front of the convenience store, at noon. I'll come in my car.

lines.t: Parfait, ça va être le fun !
lines.n: Perfect, it's going to be fun!

stress.t: On se voit en fin de semaine ?
stress.n: Shall we meet at the weekend?
stress.mark: On se voit en fin de se*maine* ?
stress.note: As everywhere in French, the last syllable of the group carries the stress; a Québec question often ends on a clear rise.

lessons.title: Belgium, Switzerland, the South, Africa
lessons.goal: Recognise accents and number words across the francophonie.

tip.title: Many accents, one language
tip.body: Belgium and Switzerland say septante (70) and nonante (90); in some Swiss cantons (Vaud, Valais, Fribourg) you also hear huitante (80), while Belgians say quatre-vingts. Swiss French is often perceived as slower, with some vowels drawn out; many Belgian and Swiss speakers keep distinctions Paris has largely lost, such as brin vs brun. In southern France the final e is often pronounced (une petite ≈ "u-ne pe-ti-te") and nasal vowels end in a light "ng" (pain ≈ "peng", demain ≈ "de-meng"). In many West African varieties the r tends to be made with the tongue tip, sometimes rolled, and syllables tend to carry more even weight.

story.title: Numbers and meals
story.intro: Charline from Liège and Fabrice from Lausanne compare how they talk.

lines.name: Charline
lines.t: Moi, je suis de Liège. Chez nous, on dit septante et nonante.
lines.n: I'm from Liège. Where I live, we say septante and nonante.

lines.name: Fabrice
lines.t: Nous aussi, à Lausanne. Et pour quatre-vingts, on dit souvent huitante.
lines.n: Us too, in Lausanne. And for eighty, we often say huitante.

lines.name: Charline
lines.t: Ah non, ça, en Belgique, on ne le dit pas. Mais à midi, on dîne, et le soir, on soupe !
lines.n: Oh no, we don't say that in Belgium. But at noon we have dîner, and in the evening we have souper!

lines.name: Fabrice
lines.t: Exactement comme chez nous. Tu me donnes ton numéro de portable ?
lines.n: Exactly like us. Will you give me your mobile number?

lines.name: Charline
lines.t: Bien sûr. Mon numéro de GSM finit par septante-deux, nonante-trois.
lines.n: Of course. My mobile number ends in seventy-two, ninety-three.

prompts.n: Say "ninety" the Belgian or Swiss way.
